name: google/double-conversion
baseline: std::ostringstream (iostreams); page's headline ratio is vs sprintf()
workload: RandomDigit case: convert 1,000 random doubles (1-17 significant decimal digits) to shortest round-trippable ASCII string, min of 10 trials x100 iterations each.
claimed_speedup: 6.23x faster than sprintf() (verbatim, page's own Speedup column: doubleconv 201.645ns vs sprintf 1256.376ns); ~13.8x faster than std::ostringstream (derived from page data: 201.645ns vs 2,778.748ns)
compiler_and_flags: Visual C++ 2013, Win64 build (via premake4); optimization flags not stated in README
stars_or_usage: 1,194 stars; used in V8, Chromium, RapidJSON and many other JSON/serialization libraries
tradeoffs: Built as a small standalone library (not header-only), needs its own build step; C++ (extracted from V8's number conversion code); covers both double->string and string->double directions, matching std::to_chars and std::stod/from_chars.
caveats: Benchmark hardware (2009-era Core i7 920) and compiler (VC++2013) are over a decade old; explicit optimizer flags not stated so this falls short of Tier A; benchmark predates C++17 std::to_chars, so std::ostringstream (iostreams) is the only in-scope std facility with a number on the page; sprintf figure is the page's own ratio, ostringstream ratio is derived from page data.

name: fpconv (night-shift)
baseline: std::ostringstream (iostreams); page's headline ratio is vs sprintf()
workload: RandomDigit case: convert 1,000 random doubles (1-17 significant decimal digits) to shortest round-trippable ASCII string, min of 10 trials x100 iterations each.
claimed_speedup: 4.59x faster than sprintf() (verbatim, page's own Speedup column: fpconv 273.822ns vs sprintf 1256.376ns); ~10.1x faster than std::ostringstream (derived from page data: 273.822ns vs 2,778.748ns)
compiler_and_flags: Visual C++ 2013, Win64 build (via premake4); optimization flags not stated in README
tradeoffs: Tiny single .c/.h pair (Grisu2 algorithm), easy to vendor; repo also bundles an unmaintained D port; Grisu2 is not a fully-optimal algorithm (unlike Grisu3/Ryu/Schubfach) so in rare cases output is one digit longer than the true shortest representation.
caveats: Same aged hardware (Core i7 920) and compiler (VC++2013) as the shootout this is harvested from; no explicit optimizer flags stated, capping this at Tier B; small, low-activity project (62 stars).

name: stb_sprintf (nothings/stb)
workload: Formatting microbenchmarks across %d/%x/%f/%e/%g/%a/%I64d and long strings, run against the platform C runtime's sprintf implementation.
claimed_speedup: Verbatim from stb_sprintf.h header comment ("PERFORMANCE vs MSVC 2008 32-/64-bit"): "%f" across e-10..e+10 floats 7.3x/6.0x faster; "%e" 8.1x/6.0x faster; "%g" 10.0x/7.1x faster; "%.320f" near e-300 12.6x/11.2x faster; "%d" across all 32-bit ints 4.8x/4.0x faster; "...512 char string..." 35.0x/32.5x faster; text also states GCC's CRT sprintf is "even slower than MSVC" but gives no GCC numbers.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2008 (32-bit and 64-bit) as the comparison CRT; no optimization flags stated; GCC mentioned qualitatively only
stars_or_usage: 34.7k stars for the stb collection; stb_sprintf.h is widely embedded in game engines and graphics codebases
tradeoffs: Single-header, drop-in sprintf/snprintf replacement (no external deps); float formatting uses internal double-double math (~105-bit precision) for round-trip-correct output, so exact insignificant digits can differ from glibc/MSVC CRT (documented in the header) even though round-trip via atof is exact.
caveats: First-party claim in the library's own header, not an independent benchmark; comparison baseline is MSVC 2008 (very old, ~2008-era CRT) with no CPU model or optimizer flags given, and no methodology beyond the numbers themselves -- caps this at Tier C; numbers have not been refreshed for modern MSVC/glibc CRTs.

name: Eisel-Lemire fast float parsing (fastfloat/fast_float) -- Lemire 2021 peer-reviewed benchmark
workload: Parsing 64-bit floating-point numbers from decimal ASCII strings, single-threaded, across three datasets: canada (111k real-world coordinate floats from a standard JSON parsing benchmark corpus), uniform (100k random floats in [0,1]), and integer (100k random 32-bit integers formatted as text).
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (Daniel Lemire, "Number Parsing at a Gigabyte per Second", Software: Practice and Experience, 2021; arXiv:2101.11408). Table 9, AMD EPYC 7262 Zen2, GCC 10.2 -O3: this-paper's parser reaches 51-70 million numbers/s vs strtod's 9.3-24 million/s (~3-5x) and vs abseil's from_chars 21-30 million/s (~2x); text states "our approach is generally twice as fast as the abseil library and up to five times faster than the standard library." Table 13, Intel i7-7700K@4.2GHz, MSVC 19.26.28806 (VS2019): parser reaches 37-60 million numbers/s vs Microsoft's std::from_chars 6.7-22 million/s (~2.7-6.7x) and vs strtod 6.0-15 million/s (~4-8.3x). Apple M1, clang 12.0.0 -O3: parser reaches 1.5 GiB/s on the uniform dataset; text states strtod is "several times slower than any other number parser" on that platform. Big-integer test on AMD Zen2: parser exceeds 1100 MiB/s vs strtod's 110 MiB/s (~10x) and abseil's 910 MiB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Linux (4 CPU architectures): GCC 10.2, flags -O3 -DNDEBUG. Windows: Microsoft C++ compiler 19.26.28806 (Visual Studio 2019), flags /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG. macOS/Apple M1: Apple clang 12.0.0, flags -O3 -DNDEBUG.
hardware: Intel i7-6700 (Skylake, 3.7GHz); AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen2, 3.39GHz); Ampere ARM Skylark (aarch64, 3.2GHz); IBM POWER9 (ppc64le, 3.77GHz); Intel Core i7-7700K (4.2GHz, Windows run); Apple M1 (ARM, 3.2GHz) -- all named explicitly in the paper's Table 8/13.
stars_or_usage: 2,114 stars; algorithm adopted by GCC 12's runtime, Rust 1.55+, Go 1.16's strconv, Apache Arrow, Yandex ClickHouse (per paper's abstract/footnotes)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11-compliant, no heap allocation; only handles the common case (significand of <=19 digits) directly, needs a documented fallback for pathological many-digit inputs (a 2022 follow-up paper, arXiv:2212.06644, proves that fallback path is in fact unreachable); same Eisel-Lemire algorithm also shipped as lemire/fast_double_parser (also on the exclusion list) and ported to Rust/C#/Java per the paper's footnotes.
caveats: This is a Tier-A peer-reviewed/published benchmark (public benchmark repo https://github.com/lemire/simple_fastfloat_benchmark tag v0.1.0, plus compiler, flags and CPU model all stated for every platform) for a project already on the exclusion list, reported per the KNOWN_LIST exception for Tier A/B academic evidence; repo_url points at fastfloat/fast_float, the implementation the paper itself cites (footnote 7) as its open-source library.
